paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לְנֹ֔חַ בֹּֽא־אַתָּ֥ה וְכָל־בֵּיתְךָ֖ אֶל־הַתֵּבָ֑ה כִּֽי־אֹתְךָ֥ רָאִ֛יתִי צַדִּ֥יק לְפָנַ֖י בַּדּ֥וֹר הַזֶּֽה׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to Noah, "Come — you and all your household — into the ark; for I have seen you righteous before me in this generation.

paragraphs.text: מִכֹּ֣ל ׀ הַבְּהֵמָ֣ה הַטְּהוֹרָ֗ה תִּֽקַּח־לְךָ֛ שִׁבְעָ֥ה שִׁבְעָ֖ה אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשְׁתּ֑וֹ וּמִן־הַבְּהֵמָ֡ה אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹ֣א טְהֹרָ֥ה הִ֛וא שְׁנַ֖יִם אִ֥ישׁ וְאִשְׁתּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Of every clean animal you shall take with you seven pairs, male and his female; and of every animal that is not clean, two, male and his female;

paragraphs.commentary:
**Two textual seams at once.**

First, the count contradicts 6:19–20, which instructed Noah to bring *two of each* — without the clean/unclean distinction. Here in 7:2 a finer instruction is given: seven pairs of clean animals, two of unclean. The two instructions reflect different source-strands in the documentary hypothesis (P at 6:19–20; J at 7:2–3). The redactor preserved both side-by-side. The common harmonization: the second instruction is the *specific override* for clean animals, with the general two-of-each rule running underneath.

Second, the clean / unclean (*tahor* / *lo tahor*) categories appear *before* the Sinai legislation (Lev 11) that codifies them. The chapter assumes both Noah and the reader know which animals fall in each category. Genesis repeatedly assumes Sinai-categorized phenomena in pre-Sinai narrative: sabbath in 2:2–3, sacrifice in 4:3–5, circumcision (still ahead) in 17. The narrative writes from a post-Sinai standpoint into a pre-Sinai world without flagging the anachronism.

paragraphs.text: גַּ֣ם מֵע֧וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֛יִם שִׁבְעָ֥ה שִׁבְעָ֖ה זָכָ֣ר וּנְקֵבָ֑ה לְחַיּ֥וֹת זֶ֖רַע עַל־פְּנֵ֥י כָל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: Also of the birds of the skies — seven pairs, male and female — to keep seed alive on the face of all the land.

paragraphs.text: כִּי֩ לְיָמִ֨ים ע֜וֹד שִׁבְעָ֗ה אָֽנֹכִי֙ מַמְטִ֣יר עַל־הָאָ֔רֶץ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים י֔וֹם וְאַרְבָּעִ֖ים לָ֑יְלָה וּמָחִ֗יתִי אֶֽת־כָּל־הַיְקוּם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשִׂ֔יתִי מֵעַ֖ל פְּנֵ֥י הָֽאֲדָמָֽה׃

i18n.en: For in seven more days I will cause it to rain on the land for forty days and forty nights; and I will wipe out every living thing that I have made from the face of the ground."

paragraphs.commentary:
**Two periods named in one verse.** *Seven more days* (until the Flood begins) plus *forty days and forty nights* (the rainfall duration). The seven-day countdown is a *small* grace-period — just enough time to finish loading the ark. The forty-day rainfall is the chapter's central duration. Forty days will return as a structural unit at 8:6 (the wait before opening the window). The number forty, here in its first chronological function in Genesis, will recur throughout the Hebrew Bible as a structural duration: forty years in the wilderness (Numbers 14, 32), forty days on Sinai (Ex 24:18), forty days of Goliath's challenge (1 Sam 17:16), forty days of Jesus' wilderness fast (Mt 4:2). The number's *fortyness* is a duration-unit, not a calendrical fact.

*Umachiti* — *and I will wipe out* — recurs the verb of 6:7. The intention is again *erasure*, not destruction-by-force.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֖עַשׂ נֹ֑חַ כְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֖הוּ יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: Noah did all that YHWH commanded him.

paragraphs.text: וְנֹ֕חַ בֶּן־שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת שָׁנָ֑ה וְהַמַּבּ֣וּל הָיָ֔ה מַ֖יִם עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: Noah was six hundred years old when the deluge of waters came upon the land.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֣בֹא נֹ֗חַ וּ֠בָנָיו וְאִשְׁתּ֧וֹ וּנְשֵֽׁי־בָנָ֛יו אִתּ֖וֹ אֶל־הַתֵּבָ֑ה מִפְּנֵ֖י מֵ֥י הַמַּבּֽוּל׃

i18n.en: Noah came into the ark — and his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives with him — because of the waters of the deluge.

paragraphs.text: מִן־הַבְּהֵמָה֙ הַטְּהוֹרָ֔ה וּמִן־הַ֨בְּהֵמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֵינֶ֖נָּה טְהֹרָ֑ה וּמִ֨ן־הָע֔וֹף וְכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־רֹמֵ֖שׂ עַל־הָֽאֲדָמָֽה׃

i18n.en: Of the clean animals, and of the animals that are not clean, and of the birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground —

paragraphs.text: שְׁנַ֨יִם שְׁנַ֜יִם בָּ֧אוּ אֶל־נֹ֛חַ אֶל־הַתֵּבָ֖ה זָכָ֣ר וּנְקֵבָ֑ה כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֶת־נֹֽחַ׃

i18n.en: they came to Noah into the ark, two by two, male and female, as the Elohim commanded Noah.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֖י לְשִׁבְעַ֣ת הַיָּמִ֑ים וּמֵ֣י הַמַּבּ֔וּל הָי֖וּ עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: After the seven days, the waters of the deluge came upon the land.

paragraphs.text: בִּשְׁנַ֨ת שֵׁשׁ־מֵא֤וֹת שָׁנָה֙ לְחַיֵּי־נֹ֔חַ בַּחֹ֙דֶשׁ֙ הַשֵּׁנִ֔י בְּשִׁבְעָֽה־עָשָׂ֥ר י֖וֹם לַחֹ֑דֶשׁ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֗ה נִבְקְעוּ֙ כָּֽל־מַעְיְנֹת֙ תְּה֣וֹם רַבָּ֔ה וַאֲרֻבֹּ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם נִפְתָּֽחוּ׃

i18n.en: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month — on this very day — all the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the floodgates of the skies were opened.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The reversal of Day Two and Day Three.** Two cosmic barriers fail simultaneously. From below: *kol maayanot t'hom rabbah nivqe'u* — *all the fountains of the great deep burst open*. From above: *arubot ha-shamayim niftachu* — *the floodgates of the skies were opened*.

Reading back to Genesis 1: on Day Two (1:6–8) the *raqia* (dome) was made *to separate* the upper waters from the lower waters; the upper waters now pour down through opened floodgates. On Day Three (1:9–10) the lower waters were *gathered to one place* so dry land could appear; those waters now burst forth from below. The Flood is, in the chapter's grammar, the *un-doing* of the second and third days of creation. The boundary-keeping work of Day Two is reversed (raqia is breached); the gathering-work of Day Three is reversed (waters released back).

*T'hom rabbah* — *the great deep* — is the same noun (*t'hom*) that named the primordial waters in 1:2 ('darkness was over the face of *the deep*'). The cognate of Akkadian *tiāmtu*, the same root behind *Tiamat* of the *Enuma Elish*. Genesis 1 demythologized the deep; Genesis 7 has it bursting forth again. The chapter is *invoking* the cosmic-primordial water that was supposedly sealed by the creation week.

The specific date — year 600 of Noah, second month, seventeenth day — is the *first absolute date* in the Hebrew Bible. The narrative cares about calendrical precision: this is a one-time event with a recorded start-time, not a mythic eternal-recurrence. The Flood narrative spans about a year in the chapter's chronology (from 7:11 to 8:14 — a solar year plus 11 days, matching the lunar/solar calendar gap).

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֥י הַגֶּ֖שֶׁם עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים י֔וֹם וְאַרְבָּעִ֖ים לָֽיְלָה׃

i18n.en: The rain was upon the land forty days and forty nights.

paragraphs.text: בְּעֶ֨צֶם הַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ בָּ֣א נֹ֔חַ וְשֵׁם־וְחָ֥ם וָיֶ֖פֶת בְּנֵי־נֹ֑חַ וְאֵ֣שֶׁת נֹ֗חַ וּשְׁלֹ֧שֶׁת נְשֵֽׁי־בָנָ֛יו אִתָּ֖ם אֶל־הַתֵּבָֽה׃

i18n.en: On that very same day Noah came in — and Shem, Ham, and Yafet, Noah's sons, and Noah's wife, and the three wives of his sons with them — into the ark,

paragraphs.text: הֵ֜מָּה וְכָל־הַֽחַיָּ֣ה לְמִינָ֗הּ וְכָל־הַבְּהֵמָה֙ לְמִינָ֔הּ וְכָל־הָרֶ֛מֶשׂ הָרֹמֵ֥שׂ עַל־הָאָ֖רֶץ לְמִינֵ֑הוּ וְכָל־הָע֣וֹף לְמִינֵ֔הוּ כֹּ֖ל צִפּ֥וֹר כָּל־כָּנָֽף׃

i18n.en: they and every wild animal according to its kind, and every domesticated animal according to its kind, and every creeping thing that creeps on the land according to its kind, and every bird according to its kind — every bird, every winged thing.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ אֶל־נֹ֖חַ אֶל־הַתֵּבָ֑ה שְׁנַ֤יִם שְׁנַ֙יִם֙ מִכָּל־הַבָּשָׂ֔ר אֲשֶׁר־בּ֖וֹ ר֥וּחַ חַיִּֽים׃

i18n.en: They came to Noah into the ark, two by two, of all flesh in which is the breath of life.

paragraphs.text: וְהַבָּאִ֗ים זָכָ֨ר וּנְקֵבָ֤ה מִכָּל־בָּשָׂר֙ בָּ֔אוּ כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה אֹת֖וֹ אֱלֹהִ֑ים וַיִּסְגֹּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה בַּֽעֲדֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Those that came in, male and female of all flesh, came in as the Elohim had commanded him; and YHWH closed him in.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The hand at the door.** The verse closes with a tender, almost domestic gesture: *vayisgor YHWH baado* — *and YHWH closed him in*. The verb סָגַר sagar (qal, transitive) takes YHWH as subject — not Noah, not a generic 'it was closed'. YHWH personally seals the ark from the outside. The preposition בְּעַד baad ('behind, for the protection of, on behalf of') gives the act a *custodial* register — YHWH is taking custody of the closing.

The chapter's *covenant* (6:18) is enacted here in a single gesture. Inside: Noah, his family, the animals. Outside: YHWH. Between: a sealed door. The Flood will commence in the next verse; before it does, the closure-of-protection is made personally. Note the divine-name shift: the same verse calls God *Elohim* (in the commanding) and *YHWH* (in the closing) — the chapter is moving between the two names in close proximity, as the documentary hypothesis would predict from a redacted P + J seam, and as the chapter's own grammar absorbs without comment.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֧י הַמַּבּ֛וּל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים י֖וֹם עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִּרְבּ֣וּ הַמַּ֗יִם וַיִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת־הַתֵּבָ֔ה וַתָּ֖רָם מֵעַ֥ל הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: The deluge was on the land forty days; the waters increased and lifted up the ark, and it rose above the land.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגְבְּר֥וּ הַמַּ֛יִם וַיִּרְבּ֥וּ מְאֹ֖ד עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ הַתֵּבָ֖ה עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַמָּֽיִם׃

i18n.en: The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the land, and the ark went on the face of the waters.

paragraphs.text: וְהַמַּ֗יִם גָּֽבְר֛וּ מְאֹ֥ד מְאֹ֖ד עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיְכֻסּ֗וּ כָּל־הֶֽהָרִים֙ הַגְּבֹהִ֔ים אֲשֶׁר־תַּ֖חַת כָּל־הַשָּׁמָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: The waters prevailed more and more upon the land, and all the high mountains under all the skies were covered.

paragraphs.text: חֲמֵ֨שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה אַמָּה֙ מִלְמַ֔עְלָה גָּבְר֖וּ הַמָּ֑יִם וַיְכֻסּ֖וּ הֶהָרִֽים׃

i18n.en: The waters prevailed fifteen cubits upward, and the mountains were covered.

paragraphs.commentary: **A draft of fifteen cubits.** The ark's height was thirty cubits (6:15). The water rises *fifteen* cubits above the highest mountains. Rashi reads the symmetry: the ark sat in the water at half its height — fifteen cubits submerged, fifteen above the surface — and floated *exactly* clearing the highest peaks below. The mountains pass under the ark with the precise clearance of its draft. The chapter does not comment on its own arithmetic; the geometry is left for the reader to assemble.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגְוַ֞ע כָּל־בָּשָׂ֣ר ׀ הָרֹמֵ֣שׂ עַל־הָאָ֗רֶץ בָּע֤וֹף וּבַבְּהֵמָה֙ וּבַ֣חַיָּ֔ה וּבְכָל־הַשֶּׁ֖רֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵ֣ץ עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וְכֹ֖ל הָאָדָֽם׃

i18n.en: All flesh that moved on the land perished — birds, cattle, wild animals, every swarming creature that swarms on the land — and every human.

paragraphs.commentary: **The verb of quiet death.** *Vayigwa* — *expired* — is distinct from the generic verb for *dying*. The same verb is used in the Hebrew Bible for the patriarchs' deaths: Abraham *expired* and was gathered to his people (Gen 25:8); Isaac *expired* (35:29); Jacob *expired* (49:33). In each case the register is full-of-years, peaceful, gathered-to-kin. Here the same verb is applied at mass scale: *vayigwa kol basar* — all flesh expired. The chapter chooses a vocabulary of peaceful expiration to report a violent mass extinction. The narrative refuses spectacle; it lists categories (birds, cattle, wild animals, swarmers, humans) in the order of 1:20–26, and reports that all of them have expired.

paragraphs.text: כֹּ֡ל אֲשֶׁר֩ נִשְׁמַת־ר֨וּחַ חַיִּ֜ים בְּאַפָּ֗יו מִכֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר בֶּחָֽרָבָ֖ה מֵֽתוּ׃

i18n.en: Everything in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, of all that was on the dry ground, died.

paragraphs.commentary: **The reversal of 2:7.** The phrase נִשְׁמַת רוּחַ חַיִּים *nishmat ruach chayim* unusually doubles the breath-vocabulary, pairing *neshamah* with *ruach*. Compare 2:7, where YHWH-Elohim breathed *nishmat chayim* (breath of life) into the human's nostrils, *and the human became a living being*. Here in 7:22 the same vocabulary is used in reverse: *everything in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life — died*. The animation-by-breath of 2:7 is undone by the un-breath of 7:22. The chapter is reversing creation's specific act of inspiration.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּ֜מַח אֶֽת־כָּל־הַיְק֣וּם ׀ אֲשֶׁ֣ר ׀ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה מֵאָדָ֤ם עַד־בְּהֵמָה֙ עַד־רֶ֙מֶשׂ֙ וְעַד־ע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיִּמָּח֖וּ מִן־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִשָּׁ֧אֶר אַךְ־נֹ֛חַ וַֽאֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בַּתֵּבָֽה׃

i18n.en: He wiped out every living thing on the face of the ground — from human to cattle, to creeping thing, to bird of the skies — they were wiped out from the land. Only Noah remained, and those with him in the ark.

paragraphs.commentary:
**The remnant.** The verse closes the chapter with the word that will become a major theological term: *vayisha'er ach Noach* — *only Noah remained*. The verb שָׁאַר sha'ar (here in the niphal: *was left, remained*) is the lexical family of שְׁאֵרִית she'erit — the *remnant* — the technical term in later prophetic literature for the surviving faithful few preserved through national catastrophe (Isa 10:20–22, Mic 2:12, Jer 31:7, Zeph 3:13). Genesis 7:23 stands at the *origin* of the Hebrew Bible's remnant-theology: a faithful core preserved through total destruction.

The verse also closes the chapter's wiping-vocabulary: the verb *machah* — wipe, erase, blot out — appears twice in active and passive: *vayyimach* ('he wiped') and *vayyimmachu* ('they were wiped'). The wiping that v4 announced is completed here. The chapter ends with the verb of erasure achieved, and the remnant clause attached.

The restrictive adverb אַךְ ach ('only, just') frames the verse with its key image: from total population to *only Noah*. The thread of preservation has narrowed to a single household in a sealed wooden box on top of an ocean that has covered the highest mountains.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגְבְּר֥וּ הַמַּ֖יִם עַל־הָאָ֑רֶץ חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים וּמְאַ֖ת יֽוֹם׃

i18n.en: The waters prevailed upon the land one hundred and fifty days.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter ends suspended.** No release, no recession, no dove yet — just the duration. *Chamishim u-meat yom* — 150 days of prevailing waters. The chapter ends with the picture: a single floating ark on a sea over a buried world, day 150 of the prevailing. The next chapter opens with *vayyizkor Elohim et Noach* — *and the Elohim remembered Noah*. The 150 days are the longest stretch of the Flood narrative without a single divine action recorded. The chapter lets the silence stand.
